title: In Defense of Micromanagement
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien reclaims the instinct beneath the micromanagement insult: the impulse to notice when small things have drifted from standard and to move them back — quietly, consistently, without drama. Using restaurateur Pat Cetta's saltshaker lesson (taught through Danny Meyer's Setting the Table), O'Brien argues that entropy is permanent and consistent pressure to correct it is not micromanagement but essential operational leadership. The label 'micromanagement' is typically applied to a specific failure mode — controlling, anxious, tedious intervention in others' decisions — but the underlying impulse (noticing drift and restoring standard) is entirely correct. O'Brien's concept of 'constant, gentle pressure' is borrowed from chef Michael Chiarello: all three words matter, and the failure of most leaders is in dropping either 'constant' (they notice but don't act) or 'gentle' (they act but with drama rather than quiet expectation). The essay connects this to school leadership specifically, where the thousand-saltshaker problem — keeping standards alive across many classrooms and many interactions — is exactly the operational challenge of principals and instructional leaders.
points: The saltshaker metaphor is the article's most memorable tool: standards drift constantly because entropy is permanent, and the leader's job is to notice the drift and restore the standard — every time, without exception, without drama.

'Constant, gentle pressure' captures the leadership discipline more precisely than any alternatives: removing 'constant' produces episodic enforcement that staff learn to game; removing 'gentle' produces anxious, reputation-damaging intervention.

The fear of the micromanagement label causes many leaders to avoid the essential work of noticing drift and correcting it — which means the insult is itself causing the operational failure it appears to condemn.

The essay's key distinction is between the failure mode called micromanagement (controlling decisions, second-guessing judgment, approving fonts) and the correct instinct beneath it (restoring standards that have drifted from expectation).

In school leadership, the thousand-saltshaker problem is the whole job: maintaining instructional standards, behavioral expectations, and cultural norms across many classrooms requires the same constant, gentle, non-dramatic pressure that Cetta demonstrated with a single shaker.
quotes: It’s one of the few leadership insults that lands the same way in a school, a restaurant, or a Fortune 500 office. Say it in a meeting and everyone nods, like you’ve named a disease.

The saltshaker There’s a piece in Danny Meyers’s book Setting the Table that I think about constantly. (Credit to my long-time boss, mentor, friend John McBride for putting this in front of me.) Meyers was a first-time restaurant owner struggling to hold his staff to any consistent standard.

A hundred small unaddressed ones erode it, and nobody can point to the day it happened, because there wasn’t one. There was just a long stretch of days when somebody walked past the saltshaker instead of resetting it.

What we’re actually avoiding Most managers who skip the small stuff aren’t following some enlightened, hands-off philosophy. They’re following the path of least discomfort: A comment about someone’s tone in a meeting feels petty to bring up on its own.
The one where the employee, who was never once told any of this mattered, understandably feels blindsided. Not because the manager was cruel, but because the manager mistook silence for kindness.
This kind protects something different: whether the standard survives. It only works, though, if it holds to all three of Chiarello’s words.
Constant without gentle becomes exhausting and eventually resented. Gentle without constant becomes a mixed message, and your team stops believing the standard is real.
